Top of page

Louise Collier leads young "Belles" to a team win

2 December 2000, Women's Surrey CC League Race 2, Lightwater Country Park, Woking.

Louise Collier again led home the field in the League’s youngest age group – the under 13s. Her winning margin of 23 seconds over this shorter than normal course meant that for much of the race she was out of sight of the chasing bunch. Unlike the race at Tilford, however, this time Louise had team mates highly placed to back her up and with J.Massey in second place and Lizzy Hodges in fourth, the team scored a great win over Guildford & Godalming. As a squad they moved up into 3rd place overall behind Sutton & District and Dorking & Mole Valley.

The seniors didn’t have quite such a happy time with rivals Tania Sturton and Syreeta Stracey being the only two Belgrave runners to squeeze into the top 30. With only 10th team place on the day they slipped back down the league to 7th and now have a battle on their hands over the last two matches to ensure that they keep clear of the relegation zone.

Top of page

Thames Hare & Hounds pegged back in the Park

18 November 2000, Surrey CC League Race 2, Petersham, Richmond Park

Richmond Park was at its wettest with the Ranelagh Harriers’ regular course having to be adapted to avoid some of the flooded stretches. As the rain came on again it was heartening to see a good bunch of young runners set out around Sidmouth Wood and Queen Elizabeth’s Plantation. Team Managers Kim and Paul Collier had gathered a full team of young runners together for the Under 17/Under 15 race (all our lads being under 15) and had two more for the Under 13s. Their efforts were well rewarded with two 2nd places in the team races with young Jamie Kirton leading the team home. With half the league now gone Belgrave now lie 2nd in the oldest age group and 3rd in the youngest.

The seniors had the huge task of trying to pull Thames Hare & Hounds back after their devastating win at Brockwell Park. There were plenty of men on hand to do their best with no fewer than 27 names listed by the time the sodden declaration sheet was handed over.

Lee Hurst was among the early leaders as the field set of in the direction of White Lodge but on the return from the loop four men had broken away - Gary Staines (SLH) and Sam Haughian (Hounslow) accompanied by our own Yacin Yusuf and Yitbarak Dinku. Yacin had turned out after changing his plans to run in the European qualifying race the next day at Margate while Yitbarak was having his first race in 10 months: we were glad to see both of them! Non-scoring Richard Ashe was close behind while Lee and Paul Freary were running together with 18 year-old Richard Ward, running his first Surrey League race in claret & gold, keeping an eye on them.

Setting out again, the positions were pretty much unchanged. A whole posse of Thames men came through together in the ‘teens but with five men in the 20s to back up our high-placers a win looked safely on the cards. Richard Hayman was not looking too comfortable but those “toughies” Rob McHarg, Will Cockerell and Joachim Wolf were running strongly with Norwegian Knut Hegvold also making an impression.

At the finish Hounslow’s Sam Haughian was an easy winner but the broadest grin came from Yacin who kept a one second margin between himself and our life-member Gary Staines. Yitbarak was so impressive in his first race of the season and he has every intention of improving on his 4th place in the races to come. As normal a blistering sprint gained Will Cockerell an extra place just inches before the finishing funnel was reached and another to run way above expectations was Phil Carstairs who had great pleasure in pushing the “Skipper”, not having a happy run, back to 10th scoring position.

Ten men home in 39; a pleasing win and 64 points pulled back on our rivals. Another one like that after Christmas and the final race would promise to be exciting.

Top of page

Thin on the ground

11 November 2000, South of Thames “Junior” 5 miles Cross-Country, Lloyd Park.

On a day of cold rain with the wind battering the runners and turning the spectators’ umbrellas inside out we were not sure that we’d be able to turn out four men to make up a team but not only did we achieve that, we ended up not so far off the medals. Policeman Rob Harding turned up in spite of being “on nights” and Jerome Curtat, now living in Paris but on a flying visit to London to see his brother, had thoughtfully brought his kit with him.

South London’s Stuart Major was in a class apart and took an early lead which rapidly grew until he was lost to sight by the main field. Our own Joachim Wolf led the Belgrave line-up and after a mile or so he was placing 4th with Rob leading the rest of the team in the early 20s. With the exception of Warren Lynch, however, the conditions took their toll on our lads over the second circuit with Joachim encountering stomach problems and Rob and Jerome drifting back somewhat. Long distance man Warren seemed to revel in the circumstances. The further the race went, the stronger he looked. Another couple of laps would have suited him fine and we relished the thought of seeing how he would tackle 9 miles of Parliament Hill mud in January!

Top of page

Back to the engravers!

04 November 2000, Reigate Priory Men’s 6 x 2.5 miles & Women’s 3 x 2.5 miles CC Relays, Priory Park, Reigate.

A sunny day in Reigate’s Priory Park was a welcome change from the recent stormy weather. Three full Belgrave teams were in action and the Belles set the ball rolling in the first race where Tania Sturton clocked the fastest Belgrave time on the initial stage. Her 9th place was maintained by Debbie Hearn and Syreeta Stracey to the finish.

As last year’s champions our men had returned the winners’ shield, freshly engraved, but were not too certain about being able to take it home again, especially when three of the A squad became unavailable at the last minute as a result of niggling injuries, etc. Kevin Quinn was desperate to run but knee pains meant that there was a strong possibility of him having to “shut off” power during the race – so down to the Bs he went. Our A squad contained not one of the six who ran so well in the previous week’s National Road Relay and, moreover, only one man from the previous year’s winning Priory team.

South London’s Robbie James took the initiative on stage one and built up a huge lead over Brighton & Hove who were being chased by two Belgrave men who were racing neck and neck to get into the top three. Eighteen year-old Frenchman Fabien Bernard-Gaudin, still without first team eligibility, led around the park and into the straight but Joachim Wolf had no intention of leaving things that way and closed him down to squeeze the A team ahead by inches at the takeover.

SLH’s challenge faded on stage two as the red vested Brighton men took control. Our own Najibe Hliouat, running more consistently and getting better very time out, worked hard and moved into second but the order changed again on stage three when Boxhill’s Paul Hayward not surprisingly got the better of Cap’n Roger, just back from honeymooning in Australia.

Brighton were 28 seconds ahead of the Bels. going into the second half of the race and with ‘super vet’ Nigel Gates their next man, no doubt were hoping to increase that margin. But Kevin Nash, our sole survivor from the team of ’99 had other ideas. It had been another week of 100 miles for ‘Gnasher’ but it didn’t seem to slow him any and while Gates pulled Brighton further away from the main body of the field our boy closed in on him until the gap was just 13 seconds with two laps remaining.

With the next team, Boxhill, now nearly two minutes behind, Will “Billy the Kid” Cockerell showed great confidence by moving up and forging a small lead. Back came the Brighton man during the desperate descent down that treacherous gully but Will opened up again and stormed the final part of the lap to give Andy Brown a 10 second advantage.

Now, with a raft of 1:50-1:51 800s under his belt, no-one doubted Andy’s ability to deliver a winning kick should the situation arise but we were rather hoping that it wouldn’t get that close. In fact it didn’t. Two and a half miles is somewhat further than our man is used to racing he was able to increase our lead by a further 8 seconds by the finish. Dave Taylor obliterated the day’s previous best times with a charge that took Herne Hill from 5th to 3rd but on this occasion we were far enough away to avoid even feeling the draught.

Back to the engravers again!

Top of page

Surely those National Medals are going to come soon!

28 October, National 6 x 5.5 kms Road Relay Sutton Park, Sutton Coldfield

On a day when Sutton Park was blasted with tree splitting winds and driving rain we overcame a disastrous start to get up to 6th – one minute and one second away from bronze – and hang on to our unofficial title of leading Southern Club – just! Drifts of sodden autumn leaves were plastered to the roadway to make the footing treacherous and in these conditions, with winds gusting to 60 mph and the linked metal railings along the course getting bowled over, individual times meant very little when compared to those of earlier years. Stages two and three probably had to face the worst of it but generally it was felt that the circumstances added around 30 seconds to what would normally be expected. The Belgrave FILA tent made its debut and what a good job it did even if, during the post race tea and cake ritual, the whole team had to hold on to the roof to stop the claret and gold pavilion taking off and heading for Lichfield.

With just 30 minutes left before the start and the team manager taking initial steps in a team reshuffle, our two first leg runners arrived, having been held up on the motorway due to the conditions. Jason Lobo had been suffering from a cold the previous week in Ireland but he had run so well there on the opening leg that we felt sure he would give us the start we needed. Poor old Jason! Everything conspired to hit him at once – the late arrival, the head cold, the previous weekend’s two races … After staying in the bunch for the first half of stage one where he was only 6 seconds off the lead, he then found himself running into big trouble and had to suffer the indignity of streams of runners overtaking him as he grimly made his way to the finish. “If it hadn’t been a relay I would have dropped out,” was his comment after he’d sent Charles Herrington on his way. An opening 39th place was not what we were looking for in our bid to get near the medals.

Charlie is working back to full fitness after the stress fracture that kept him out of action for half of the summer. Not only did he pull back seven teams and duck under 18 minutes – no mean achievement on this day – he also moved up on a whole posse of runners ahead of him to give Lee Hurst the task of picking them off. Back after a break from running, Lee duly obliged and although not happy with his time, a final position at least near to the top ten began to look possible.

One man who is in much better shape than the same time last year is Spencer Barden. Taking things steadily up the hill he then used the wind to its full advantage and blasted through the field before taking another “easy” spell and then turning it on again for the finish. Result: equal 6th fastest of the day and a time more than ten seconds faster than 1999. The rest of our guys who ran last year were between 30 and 60 seconds slower! It was a perfect run for Spenny. We had planned that he might pull us into 3rd spot at this point – and had all other things been equal he may well have done it.

Yacin Yusuf followed up by taking another five places and for the first time we went into the top ten and overtook our local rivals Thames Hare & Hounds right on the line with one stage remaining. How the slightly built Yacin managed to keep going in the gale is a marvel. It was all up to Alaster Stewart now and he didn’t disappoint with one of his best ever runs around the circuit. Two more teams fell to his stride and with a thumbs up sign as he passed our supporters at the tent in the finishing straight he, and we, were delighted with our final position.

So, time to reflect: the autumn road relays were over and we had progressed well. Second best in Surrey, 4th best in the Southern with the Surrey victors behind us, 6th best in the country with every one of the Southern clubs behind us.

Top of page

22 October 2000, Lisburn AC 5 km races, Lisburn, Northern Ireland.

Dash for the cash

The top runners from the previous day’s relay were all invited to take part in the Invitation 5 kms. After sizing up the opposition (mostly Belgrave) Morgan made a pretty shrewd move by opting instead for the open race and he proved too much of a handful for our own Kevin Nash who nevertheless ran a good race with a powerful finish to gain second.

The invitation event bore a striking resemblance to an old fashioned Belgrave club championship with all six of our relay runners in the small line-up. The weather was by now cold, gusty and rainy as Yacin Yusuf, the smallest man in the field, took the pack off the highway and into the park. Nothing changed really until the last of the four circuits when Spencer took off like a scalded cat in his dash for the cash. Yacin held up well to stay ahead of the rest as Belgrave runners took the bulk of the prizes.

Open Race: 1, M.Morgan (Finn Valley AC) 15:01; 2, K.Nash (Belgrave) 15:11; 3, A.McCullough (N.Belfast).

Top of page

Irish eyes were not the only ones smiling when the winning Belgrave team collected their prizes at Wallace Park, Lisburn. Rob McHarg, Paul Freary, Alaster Stewart, Yacin Yusuf (crouching), Jason Lobo and Spencer Barden enjoy being Irish Road Relay Champions. Photo by Leo Coy.

Road relay runners strike a winning note

21 October 2000, Lisburn AC’s 6 x 3.3 kms Road Relay inc. Irish Champs., Lisburn, Northern Ireland.

This was the 40th running of Lisburn AC’s relay and the local club’s organiser Glen Grant had managed to persuade FILA and the Lisburn Borough Council to sponsor the event and turn it into something really special. Teams were invited from the Republic of Ireland, Scotland, England and Wales and the event also incorporated the Athletic Association of Ireland’s Championship. The men’s relay was just one event on a two day program that featured 13 races and the total prize money available was no less than £10,000. Above all the organisation by Glen and his friendly crew was superb; our thanks to them for terrific weekend.

When our team gathered in the hotel lounge the evening before the relay there was much deliberation regarding the running order, additionally complicated by the fact that Messrs. Lobo and Freary had turned up with colds. In the end the consensus was that we would turn out our men in order of increasing strength. With that matter resolved, minds then turned to the prediction of individual and team times and after the runners turned in for the night it soon became noticeable that those whose cerebral machinery had been most thoroughly lubricated with Guinness came up with the fastest clockings! All seemed pretty certain that we would win.

Saturday afternoon and a superb autumn day with the bluest of skies saw 21 teams set out around Lisburn’s Wallace Park. Each stage took in three circuits of a 1.1 km course which could easily be bisected by the fitter spectators. Among unfamiliar team colours Jason Lobo’s claret and

gold vest was immediately identified as he followed early leader Fisher of Willowfield. Clonliffe’s Noel Cullen burst ahead on the second circuit but Jason, whose job was to bring us home in the top half dozen, was settled into the chasing bunch and far from a simple top six place, handed over to Rob McHarg in 2nd with a time that stood up as our fastest until the final stage.

Clonliffe now increased their lead. They had turned in two of the day’s quickest times but Finn Valley also came into contention thanks to a fine run by the tough Mark Morgan who battled past our own Rob.

Yet another hot run came from Clonliffe on stage 3. Finn Valley dropped back down the field behind a rock steady Alaster Stewart, only for North Belfast to scoot past and gain 2nd, 10 seconds behind the leaders. The Bels. were now 22 seconds off the pace while Scotland’s Cambuslang Harriers had moved up to 4th, just 6 seconds further adrift.

Fireworks! Throwing aside his pre-race plan to increase pace on each circuit, Paul Freary set about the men in front by clocking our two fastest lap splits to that point and then hanging on for dear life. Belgrave moved ahead for the first time but Paul’s final tour of the park was painful as he followed those two 3:10 splits with a 3:27 - our slowest of the day! He’d done the damage though and with four stages gone the Bels had 4 seconds in hand over Clonliffe and 5 seconds over North Belfast - and what a finish we had to come!

A smoothly running Yacin Yusuf opened the lead up to 28 seconds on his stint and with Spencer Barden running the fastest of the day, our advantage was over one and a quarter minutes by the time Spen raised his arms aloft at the race end. Regular winners of this event, Annandale Striders, came into the picture for the first time to get second and win the Irish Championship but the Maxwell Cup was now destined to bear a new name for the first time - Belgrave Harriers!

Top of page

Weston & Collier in good form

14 October 2000, Women's Surrey CC League Race 1, Tilford,

Forceful running came from Rachel Weston who led home the “Belles” at Tilford. Both Tania Sturton and Syreeta Stracey backed up well and as a result the team came home 5th – considerably better than last year’s initial position of 8th. Short of runners for the best of reasons – marriage and pregnancy – we may still find that we can emulate last winter’s final position of 4th in the league.

Louise Collier was outstanding in the under 13 event. It was the shortest race of the day but her winning margin of 47 seconds was the largest in all of the races. What a shame that young Lizzy Hodges was unable to run through illness. In nearly every race this summer past Lizzy has been just those few seconds behind Louise and the pair of them could form the basis of a really powerful team in the next few years.

Top of page

Up and coming runners make their mark

14 October 2000, Men's Surrey CC League Race 1, Brockwell Park

Admittedly we had already decided that this winter our priority races were to be the Southern and National Relays and Cross Country Championships and that we wouldn't let efforts to retain the league divert us from these races, but at the last minute the team manager was frantically trying to round up some extra men when it appeared that we were going to be much shorter of runners than previously anticipated. As it happened we didn’t do so badly although Thames Hare & Hounds grabbed a lead which will be very difficult to pull back.

Herne Hill’s ever-present Dave Taylor, individual winner last winter, soon showed his intentions by opening up a lead which stretched to nearly a minute by the finish. For the Bels, after one lap, Yacin Yusuf and Paul Freary were handily placed at the front of the chasing pack with a whole bunch of claret and gold vests around the 20s. A revitalised South London Harriers were being led by their Captain Stuart Major but it was already clear that Thames were the team in charge.

Going out again Major seemed to be getting the better of Freary and Yusuf who were battling with SLH’s James and Sykes with the leading Thames men also in close order. Soon, however, an ill-looking Yacin seemed to be drifting back and half a mile from the finish paid the penalty for partaking of a pre-race tuna and sweet corn sandwich – and pulled out.

Up the penultimate hill Paul Freary gained enormously and as they turned a to drop down again the Belgrave man eased right up to Major’s shoulder and seemed to be biding his time before striking out for second place but 200 metres later it was the figure in the SLH vest that had broken away by 15 metres with two more of his club mates lining themselves up for an attack on our Vice-Captain.

Now up that final drag to the finish and as white vests gained on Paul, so he gained on Stuart Major – and took him within a few metres of the finish line.

New member Fabien Bernard-Gaudin, only 18 years old, had a terrific run to gain 13th place but as an unregistered athlete could not score for us. This young Frenchman is studying at Westminster College and will be in London for a couple of years. Not far behind came Richard Hayman running his best ever race and at only a few days past his 21st birthday another great prospect.

Will Cockerell raised his game to a new level. Last winter he was the only man who scored in all four league races – usually coming home in the late 30s – and here he was on the verge of getting into the teens. A big effort came from Joachim Wolf, finishing within two seconds of training partner Rob McHarg, and outstanding efforts weren’t restricted to the scoring ten either as Adrian Jowett ran like a man possessed to put four Belgravians behind him.

It was good to see seven young Belgrave Harriers in action with Gary Mabbutt leading our young team home. Both our under 17 and under 13 teams equalled the seniors' position of 3rd.

Top of page

Upward trend continues

30 September 2000, Rushmoor Arena nr. Aldershot, South of England 6 Stage Road Relay

The upward trend in our running fortunes continued at Rushmoor Arena, near Aldershot, when the club managed to finish three teams in the South of England AA 6-Stage Road Relay Championship and claim our best ever team performance in the event. And while the ‘A’ squad were just out of the medals, the Bels. second team made their presence felt by being the first ‘B’ team home in 14th – a position that our first team have only ever beaten once before. With a third team mostly made up of new members and two-thirds of a ‘D’ team also in action, the future is beginning to look distinctly exciting.

Borough of Hounslow AC were back in force for the event, going to the lengths of wearing t-shirts bearing the legend “The Boys Are Back In Town”, dying their hair in club colours of blue and white and wearing face paints of the same hue. They just had to win dressed like that and from Sam Haughian’s initial leg, apart from a 'blip' on stage two, they just went further and further away. Behind them the order chopped and changed until the Thames boys surprised by forcefully claiming 2nd on stage four with the always-strong Aldershot team moving into 3rd at the same point. The Bels. gradually saw off the challenges of London Irish, Blackheath, Cornwall, Southampton Runners and South London and 4th place at the end was about what we expected.

Charles Herrington set the race up nicely by placing 7th on the opening stage among teams that were mostly never going to go the whole distance at that level but the rest of the team, although occupying the race positions we were expecting, were all about 20 seconds down on predicted times. All have a lot more fitness to find yet – which is no bad thing at this stage of the season; we have a long way to go.

Rob McHarg ran himself into the ‘six’ that will compete for Belgrave in the Irish Road Relay Championships in three weeks time and two who impressed greatly in the ‘C’ team were the French U20 steeplechaser Fabien Bernard-Gaudin and Norwegian Knut Hegvold.

Teams: 1, Borough of Hounslow 1:50:39; 2, Thames Hare & Hounds 1:51:59, 3, Aldershot F&D 1:52:26; 4, Belgrave ‘A’ 1:53:43; 5, London Irish 1:54:34; dq, Southampton Runners 1:55:04; 6, Shaftesbury Barnet 1:55:15; 7 Bedford & County 1:55:24; 8, Blackheath 1:55:28; 9, South London 1:56:15; … 14, Belgrave ‘B’ 1:57:48; 31, Belgrave ‘C’ 2:02:55; 66 teams finished.

Fastest: D.Taylor (Blackheath) 17:41; M.O'Dowd (Swindon) 17:50; 3, C.Thompson (Aldershot F&D) 17:50; 4, B.Whitby (Boro' Hounslow) 17:51.

‘A’ Team : C.Herrington (7) 18:25 ; R.Alsop (10) 19:26 ; Y.Yusuf (6) 18:49 ; R.McHarg (6) 19:15 ; P.Freary (5) 18:47 ; A.Hutchinson (4) 19:01 .

‘B’ Team : N.Hliouat 20:02 ; K.Nash 19:30 ; K.Quinn 19:36 ; J.Wolf 19:51 ; R.Hayman 19:38 ; W.Cockerell 19:35 .

‘C’ Team : P.Carstairs 20:28 ; F.Bernard-Gaudin 19:30 ; M.Byansi 20:26 ; B.Peeters 20:23 ; K.Hegvold 19:37 ; W.Lynch 22:31 .

‘D’ Team : E.Lemenager 20:45 ; J.Mather 23:11 ; D.Anderson 22:03; A.Jowett 23:33.

Back to Index

Top of page

Solid Surrey Silver

09 September 2000, Wimbledon Park, Surrey County AA 6 x 3 miles Road Relay

You couldn’t ask much more for the start of the “winter” season – twenty senior runners, a veterans team, a nice crowd of spectators and a general feeling that good times lie ahead. Well, alright, a win would have been nice, but all credit to a South London Harriers outfit that turned out their strongest team to carry the day. The Bels. broke the old course record – but SLH had already scorched home over 2 minutes ahead.

Several of Belgrave’s Surrey team were in far from the best of shape, Roger Alsop and Alaster Stewart just about overcoming injury, Yacin Yusuf only recently returning to running after sickness and Graham Adams and Jim Estall both having had low key summers and it was a similar story among the non-Surrey men where even Paul Freary has a fair amount of fitness to reclaim – even though he only just missed Alsop’s Belgrave best of 14:23 from 1999.

Cap’n Rog. enjoyed the first event of his stag weekend, going some 15 seconds faster than anticipated to bring the Bels home to 3rd on stage 1, while Rich. Hayman was only 10 seconds behind for the ‘B’s. Meanwhile South London had grabbed a lead they were never to relinquish and Reigate Priory were in second.

Twentyone year-old Kevin Quinn was in sparkling form on stage 2 to chop a minute off his best time round the course (he has recently recorded personal records of 1:56 and 3:59 on the track). Steve Clarke for the ‘B’s went past him up the hill but Kev was in no mood to give way and came back at his club mate once at the top. Steve’s time was Belgrave’s second fastest of the day but both runners had to give way to Herne Hill’s Boyle.

Stage 3 and an out of condition Yacin Yusuf pulled the Bels back to 2nd while Rob McHarg advanced the ‘B’ team’s cause by going into 3rd. Up front Gary Staines set the day’s fastest. It was good to see “Gerry” Adams back in the team with a solid run but Joachim Wolf took 2 seconds out of him to put the non-Surrey men just 7 seconds down.

Veteran Jim Estall gained a little ground on the leaders on the penultimate stage and handed over to Alaster Stewart whose run was another good effort after an injury-plagued summer. An unfit Simon Elliott struggled for the ‘B’s on stage 5 and Herne Hill moved into third. Paul Freary set the fastest Belgrave time of the day to try to get the ‘B’ squad back into the frame and although he caught up two whole minutes, he ran out of road with a seven second gap remaining.

Now for three weeks of solid work before tackling the SEAA 6-Stage at Aldershot on September 30th.

Senior Men: 1, South London H 87:11; 2, Belgrave ‘A’ 89:17; 3, Herne Hill 91:38; 4, Belgrave ‘B’ 91:45; 5 Boxhill R 93:53; 6, Thames H&H 96:53; 12, Belgrave ‘C’ 17:19; 20 teams started, 16 teams finished.
Fastest: G.Staines (South London) 14:09; M.Boyle (Herne Hill) & S.Major (South London) 14:14; P.McTigue (South London) 14:21; 5, P.Freary 14:24; 6, R.James (South London) 14:25.

Veteran (M40) Men: 1, South London H 63:15; 2, Thames H&H 15:47; 3, Hercules Wimbledon 65:39; 7, Belgrave 74:15.
Fastest: G.Jerwood (Herne Hill) 15:07.

Belgrave Teams:
‘A’ (Surrey) - R.Alsop 14:44; K.Quinn 14:42; Y.Yusuf 14:47; G.Adams 15:10; J.Estall (M45) 14:58; A.Stewart 14:56.
‘B’ - R.Hayman 14:54; S.Clarke 14:38; R.McHarg 14:50; J.Wolf 15:08; S. Elliott 17:51; P.Freary 14:24.
‘C’ - W.Lynch 16:47; J.Skilbeck-Nelson 17:30; M.Webb 15:49; W.Horbaczewski (M40) 19:05; B.Peeters 16:02; D.Anderson (M40) 17:19.
‘D’ - R.Harding 16:15; P.Coughlan 17:02.
Veterans - J.Mather 17:16; A.Binda 16:22; R.Bale 20:07; J.Wasbrough 21:30.

Back to Index

Top of page

Belgrave Nonsuch 4 x 2.2 miles relay

06 July 2000, Nonsuch Park

For the fourth consecutive year Belgrave notched up a win in this annual jaunt around Nonsuch Park near Cheam in Surrey - and for good measure the Bels. also won the prizes for the top veteran team.

International distance star Dave Taylor of Herne Hill led the field from the start and was 25 seconds ahead of Belgrave's Junior Galley at the first takeover. Junior confessed to having "not done a lot in training recently" but his clocking was the eighth fastest ever around the course with those seven faster times being shared by only four men. Junior's reward was a 3000 metre steeplechase spot in the following Saturday's British League team. Taylor's time was a super 10:15 and he turned out again for Herne Hill on the last stage to run another scorcher - 10:18.

On stage two Kevin Quinn reduced his best ever by 9 seconds to take the lead from the men in Red & Black and the lead was extended further by an unfit Alaster Stewart to give anchor man Will Cockerell a huge advantage. The team time was the second fastest ever.

The race was sponsored by Bill Law's company Encomech Ltd. and organised by Dave Denton. Bill is Belgrave's joint British League Team Manager.

1, Belgrave H 43:33 (J.Galley 10:40, K.Quinn 10:46, A.Stewart 10:58, W.Cockerell 11:10); 2, Guildford & Godalming 46:12; 3, Herne Hill H 47:48; ... 8, Belgrave H Veterans 49:51 (H.Corbett 13:15, A.Binda 12:00; J.Mather 12:40; D.Anderson 11:56); 46 teams finished.

Restored from the club's earlier website, belgraveharriers.com, and published here as originally written.

item.title: Bill Kerr 1932-2000
item.dc:creator: belgravearchive
item.content:encoded:
Bill Kerr (A13) hands over to Charlie Dabbs at the end of the ninth stage of the 1965 National London to Brighton Relay.

Bill Kerr died on the 15th December 2000 aged 68 years.

He was born in the Springburn area of Glasgow where his father was a Shipwright. In his early years he did very well at school where he was known as a ‘bit of a whiz kid ’ for his general knowledge. Following his school years he became an apprentice on the railway, but this career was cut short following an accident when the wheel of a steam engine dropped onto his hand, leaving him with the loss of mobility in some of his fingers for the rest of his life.

In Scotland Bill ran for Victoria Park A.A.C, and later on the Anglo Scottish Athletic Club.

However, seeking pastures new, it was in the early 1960s that Bill came south and burst upon the Belgrave scene, going on to carve himself a lifelong niche in the hearts of many of his team mates and training partners of that time.

He was a great acquisition to the Club when we badly needed one.

It is most significant that since hearing of his untimely death, the underlying memory that many of his contemporaries recall was that he was such a likeable, indeed loveable fellow. One who will always be remembered for his singular sense of humour and that mischievous look in his eyes when he related a story.

Perhaps Bill’s style and character, as well as his athletic ability, can best be illustrated by recalling the following anecdotes relayed by Clive Shippen on hearing the sad news.

" I well remember going to Belgrave Hall in March 1961 for the “five and three-quarters” road trial – a big race in those days as, generally, the first 12 were selected to carry our colours in the prestigious London to Brighton Relay which was sponsored by the News of the World.

An unfamiliar face was amongst the usual crowd of nervous runners. He had been brought along by Charlie Walker and was introduced to me as Bill Kerr, a Scotsman. Straight away he struck me as being an affable fellow with a sense of humour already apparent, and he was given permission to compete as a guest.

He was a relaxed runner with a long loping stride and he floated along just behind the leaders for most of the race. When he was sure of his way to the finish he eased ahead for a very surprising win. As you can imagine, he had a membership form in his hand before he had barely recovered his breath!

Bill was selected for the long stage 9 of the National April 1961 race. He was not familiar with the race logistics so when the Stage 9 coach dropped off it's 20 competitors and then drove straight on to the end of the stage Bill realised that his nice new Belgrave vest, complete with attached numbers, had gone with it!

I well remember a very agitated Jimmy Green (Editor of Athletics Weekly) running up to me saying ‘There's an unknown runner up ahead running in an un-numbered white vest. He took over from Jack Brown so he must be one of your's. Who the hell is he? I can't recognise him. You realise he is likely to get you disqualified’. My heart sank. Somehow we managed to get ahead of the race and notify the judges of Bill's name and number. We were not penalised, and it was an auspicious start for Bill's career with Belgrave.

Bill's best London to Brighton run was in the National event of April 1962 when he recorded 6th fastest time on the long stage 9 with only Kilby, Bullivant, Craig, Freary and Tulloh (all internationals) being faster. What is more he achieved that back in 14th place – one of our bad years.

Bill was very easy going. Nothing rattled him. Perhaps he was too easy going. His sense of humour endeared him to all. On training runs he had a habit of plucking leaves from trees and singing little ditties; alright on training runs, but very occasionally he would do so in races – very disconcerting to the other competitors!

His laid-back, easy going manner did sometimes produce anxiety in team managers. The team for the South of Thames Senior at Maidenhead in 1962 met at Paddington Station. With just 15 minutes to go before departure Bill ambled up saying, ‘I'm starving, I must get something to eat’. No sign of nerves there! I suggested that he grab a sandwich to eat on the train. With 4minutes to departure he had still not arrived at the carriage so I rushed to the station buffet fearing there must have been a mishap of some sort. Bill was casually cleaning up a plate of pie and chips! He looked up at me with that mischievous smile and said ‘What's the fuss?’ ”

Bill gained a AAA vest in 1962 and went on to become a Middlesex track champion.

Professionally Bill worked, in turn, for the Civil Service; the Anglo Iranian Oil Company as a Project Clerk ,and in latter years as a Processing Clerk for BT. Among his interests can be listed cooking, gardening a love of the music of Peggy Lee and Frank Sinatra and, when away from athletics, hockey.

In 1963 Bill ran in the Scottish National cross country championships and gained his International Vest by finishing 6th. However after the race was over he heard one of his friends bemoaning his fate at having ‘missed out again’ by finishing 7th. Whereupon Bill calmly said, “that’s OK you can have my place, ” and gave up his Vest in favour of his friend.

Such was the character of the man we will affectionately remember as Bill Kerr

Gordon Biscoe

Bill Kerr’s best track performances

1961 – 1m 4:12.8; 3km 8:21.4; 2m 8:55.0; 3m 14:04.2.

1962 – 1m 4:11.8; 2m 9:07.6; 6m 29:19.4.

1963 – 1m 4:11.6; 3km 8:05.4; 2m 8:44.6; 3m 13:46.8; 6m 29:14.2.

1964 – 2m 9:01.6. 3m 13:59.2.

1965 – 1m 4:12.8; 2m 8:53.6; 3m 13:56.8.

1966 – 2m 9:17.0; 5km 14:50.0.

1967 – 1m 4:23.8; 2m 9:03.4; 3m 14:25.8.

1968 – 1m 4:14.6; 2m 9:01.6; 3m 13:55.8; 6m 31:20.

item.title: Road Running & Cross Country Team Results January - June 2001
item.dc:creator: belgravearchive
item.content:encoded:
Back to Index

Top of page

AAA “National” 12-Stage Road Relay

What a thriller! Bels. miss the gold medals by just six seconds

Full result

28 April 2001, AAA 12-Stage Road Relay, Sutton Coldfield.

Well, we knew it was going to be exciting but who could have foreseen such a story unfolding. Team and spectators alike experienced every emotion throughout the 4 hour saga and then came that final devastating, gut-wrenching twist. As reserve Will Cockerell said afterwards, “It was almost unbelievable: but of course it wasn't unbelievable at all – just sport at its cruellest”.

Fifty-two years ago, when only 21 clubs including just five from outside the Southern area took part, Athletics Weekly described the closing stages of the 1949 National 12-Stage Road Relay with the words, “it was a grandstand finish to a race that had been close and thrilling throughout”. On that April day in 1949, on the London-Brighton road, Belgrave prevailed over Birchfield by just 20 seconds. We have never won since.

At Sutton Park in 2001, after an appalling start, a nigh-on miraculous fight-back saw us head the field for five stages – more than any other club on the day – only for the closest ever finish at Sutton Park to go against us. A blinding run from the last Tipton runner pushed the Bels. back to silver by just six seconds. It was very quiet inside the Belgrave tent for a while. The shock of having the prize snatched away just an instant after we believed for the first time that it was to be ours was stunning. This had been the target since the beginning of the season and we had come so close. But this group of runners is much more than just a team. There is a feeling for each other that rival clubs do not see when they look at Belgrave from the outside. There is no blame, anyone can have a bad run just as they can have a good one – and within 30 minutes there were already the signs of looking forward. “Right then, next year … ”

Times were affected by an icy wind which became stronger throughout the afternoon, bringing with it pulses of rain and sleet. Short stage times were down by about 10 seconds – long stages perhaps half as much again. There were 69 teams in the initial charge down the hill; 64 finished and of those 5 were disqualified – 3 of them on the 4th stage.

Stage 1

Kassa Tadesse is back as a full-time athlete having put his restaurant owning aspirations on hold for a few years. His target is now a British passport and a place in the GB half-marathon team later in the year. Six weeks of training in Kenya with John Mutai’s coach had seen him shed pounds and he looked the gaunt Kassa of 1994 where the first stage on this course had seen him come home in 1st place. Could he do it again? He hadn’t raced for around two years and had only arrived home from Nairobi the day before.

Early reports over the tannoy told us that he was lying in third place … was in the leading bunch … but he wasn’t in sight when at the end of the stage the Swansea man went through the takeover zone … or one minute later when the first dozen teams were all through … or after a further minute when we were into the thirties. It was “head in hands” time for the team-manager. Was he injured? Perhaps he wasn’t going to finish at all and 11 Belgrave runners were going to be left stranded, their day finished before it had begun.

Eventually, looking awful, Kassa came through in 35th. It transpired that he had stopped three times to vomit on the second half of the circuit and, as he barely kept moving over the last kilometre, runners had streamed past him. He was some two minutes slower than anticipated – not the sort of start we were looking for, two and a quarter minutes off the lead.

1, Swansea 25:50; 2, Trafford 25:52; 3, Mansfield 26:12; … 35, Belgrave 28:06.

Fastest: J.Lewis (Swansea) 25:50; R.Gould (Trafford) 25:52; B.Farquarson (Mansfield) 26:12; K.Tadesse 28:06 (35th).

Stage 2

Well at least it was all set up nicely for Richard Ward, youngest man in the team. He’d been warned of the possibility of receiving a forward placing and being in the firing line but here was a different scene and he adapted to it well. It was like some spectacular “shoot ‘em up” video game. In the dog-fight of this first short stage he picked off man after man whilst being subjected to the blast of runners like Telford AC’s Chris Davies who came through from 41st to 14th with the day’s fastest of 14:03. Richard thrived in all this action, taking the Bels up 15 places to clock our fastest of the day – the stage’s =6th best and =9th of the day. He enjoyed himself so much that he tells us that he has every intention of making this race a priority for the next 20 years!

Up front the race favourites Salford and Tipton were already well established in 3rd and 4th places and, in spite of Richard’s efforts, we were still 2:09 away from the leaders Trafford.

1, Trafford 40:37; 2, Bromsgrove & Redditch 41:09; 3, Salford 41:18; … 20, Belgrave 42:46.

Fastest: C.Davies (Telford) 14:03; J.Moorehouse (Birchfield) 14:15; J.Bowler (Bromsgrove & Redditch) 14:17; R.Ward 14:40 (=6th).

Stage 3

Tipton, Salford and Birchfield moved into the first three places on this second long stage and seasoned onlookers could have been forgiven for assuming that the medallists had already sorted themselves out. Not so Paul Freary: “ Ok. So it was a bad start but we’ve got 11 stages to go yet. We can get up there.” As good as his word, Paul smoothly weaved his way through the field and in a time just 1 second faster than his run of last year claimed 10 scalps and we went into the top ten, 1:14 down on the men from the Black Country. This was to have been Paul Evans’ stage but our veteran marathoner had had to pull out of the line-up with two days to go, due to post-London calf muscle problems.

1, Tipton 1:07:43; 2, Salford 1:07:50; 3, Birchfield 1:08:11; … 10, Belgrave 1:09:24.

Fastest: G.Tromans (Coventry) 26:01; B.Whitby (Windsor SE&H) 26:04; D.Taylor (Blackheath) 26:14; P.Freary 26:38 (10th).

Stage 4

A year ago 21 year-old Rick Hayman had barely started running and now, as reserve, he grabbed his chance to go into the team. An 8:47 track 3,000 metres during the week had given him confidence and he kept the forward momentum going by overtaking the blue and white vested Bedford man to move us into 9th. Announcer Bud Baldaro reminded the crowd that Belgrave had some strong long stage runners to come and knowing that some of those ahead would run out of steam soon we began to dream again of medals. Of our Southern rivals, Windsor were now in 4th, Aldershot 6th, Bedford 12th and Shaftesbury 15th.

1, Tipton 1:22:46; 2, Salford 1:22:51; 3, Birchfield 1:23:22; … 9, Belgrave 1:24:41.

Fastest: G.Cuddy (Sale) 14:30; M.Dalkins (Stoke) 14:48; R.Scanlon (Coventry) 14:49; R.Hayman 15:17 (19th).

Stage 5

There were some mean men on stage 5. Morpeth had been languishing down the field but now turned out Ian Hudspith. Birchfield’s Rob Birchall was entering the fray as was Blackheath’s first Brit home in the London Marathon, Mark Steinle. What impression could our Olympic steeplechaser Justin Chaston, with 5 hours of jet-lag in his system, make in this company? The answer: a good one. Twice stitch caused him to ease right off but he became our fastest long stage man so far and third best on the stage while overtaking Aldershot and Sale. Birchfield had grabbed a 36 second lead and we were now 2nd Southern club behind the T-shirt men Windsor SE&H, although still an agonising 1:09 off the lead.

1, Birchfield 1:49:18; 2, Tipton 1:49:54; 3, Salford 1:50:13; … 7, Belgrave 1:51:03.

Fastest: I.Hudspith (Morpeth) 25:55; R.Birchall (Birchfield) 25:56; J.Chaston 26:22.

Stage 6

Taking us to the half-way point was “Gnasher”. Kevin Nash’s coach Richard Partridge has had some glory days in Sutton Park himself and was on hand to see his protégé have a cracking run – fastest of the stage – to dispose of Windsor SE&H, Swansea and Trafford. An absolutely amazing recovery! Fourth place was now ours and the medal positions were lined up a mere 16, 22 and 49 seconds ahead with Birchfield rumoured to be running out of top men and Tipton moving back into the lead. What a race!

1, Tipton 2:04:56; 2, Salford 2:05:23; 3, Birchfield 2:05:29; 4, Belgrave 2:05:45.

Fastest: K.Nash (Belgrave) 14:42; C.Low (Shaftesbury) 14:51; N.Caddy (Tipton) 15:02.

Stage 7

Mark Miles is an awesome runner. Two years ago, at the SEAA 12-Stage, officials suggested that perhaps Mark had cut the course, so fast was his time. Co-holder of our fastest short stage time around Sutton Park (13:49) he had agreed to run a long stage if we thought it would make the difference between winning or not. We did think so – and “Milesy” went long.

Seemingly flying with feet barely touching the ground, Mark ate up Birchfield and Salford and then set about Tipton’s GB half marathon international Nick Jones. Lead motor bike, Jones and then Mark disappeared from the view of our fan-club, heading toward the furthest reach of the long stage. All eyes peered into the distance for their return. Yes. There was the headlight of the bike … and the runner behind … it was a claret vest with gold hoop. We were in the lead! Ten seconds clear at the take-over, Mark was fastest long stage man of the day and second on our all-time list only to Paul Evans.

1, Belgrave 2:31:30; 2, Tipton 2:31:40; 3, Birchfield 2:32:21.

Fastest: M.Miles (Belgrave) 25:45; J.Wild (Sale) 25:58; E.DeJonge (Shaftesbury) 26:09.

Stage 8

Talk about pressure! A pale looking Roger Alsop set off down the slope plumb in the sights of Tipton’s Seb Shepley. “I’m not worried if he comes back in 2nd,” says next man Spencer Barden, “it’ll give me someone to chase.” Someone to chase? Sorry Spen. but no such luxury as Roger proceeded to put another 11 seconds between the Bels and their green and white vested rivals. A medal of some sort now seemed a certainty with fourth place a full 1 minute and 19 seconds behind us.

1, Belgrave 2:46:36; 2, Tipton 2:46:57; 3, Birchfield 2:47:16.

Fastest: I.Gillespie (Birchfield) 14:55; R.Alsop (Belgrave) 15:06; S.Shepley (Tipton) 15:17.

Stage 9

A confident Spencer Barden with a successful winter behind him had returned from warm weather training in Portugal itching to get into this race. We needed a reasonable buffer going into the last quarter of the race – something close to a minute would be nice – and surely Spen was the man to give it to us. Working hard and setting the fastest time for the lap he levered that gap from 21 seconds up to 49. That could be just enough but my goodness this was going to be close.

1, Belgrave 3:12:56; 2, Tipton 3:13:45; 3, Birchfield 3:14:06.

Fastest: S.Barden 26:20; W.Burns (Salford) 26:46; R.Mayock (Sale) 26:48.

Stage 10

Another short stage man in the firing line, Rob McHarg had started the week looking forward to being reserve and now found himself on the tarmac, in the team, in the lead. Every second he could hold on to was crucial and he did a fine job. Tipton came up to within 15 seconds as their runner clocked a time that put him in the day’s top ten and a minute further back the battle for the bronze medal was looking ferocious as a mere 6 seconds now covered Birchfield and Salford.

1, Belgrave 3:28:10; 2, Tipton 3:28:25; 3, Birchfield 3:29:36.

Fastest: M.Hill (Tipton) 14:40; M.Moorhouse (Salford) 15:01; R.McHarg (Belgrave) 15:14.

Stage 11

The penultimate stage surely had to be the key. If Alaster Stewart could only stop Tipton’s Nigel Stirk from getting past then man for man we believed that our own Lee Hurst would be able to look after the last leg. Stirk’s pbs are somewhat faster than Alaster’s but this was our man’s 18th time of racing on the Sutton Park roadway. He knows the course like the back of his hand and it was like a dream coming true – in the lead and racing against Tipton Harriers for the most coveted trophy in Team Road Running.

The tension was really going up now. A ‘phone check with the supporters out on the course revealed that after a couple of kilometres the gap had gone up. Belgrave were now 20 seconds clear and if there was one thing we were sure of, even when well psyched up, metronome Al would never go off too fast.

Incredible. Far from stopping Stirk from getting by, at the end of the last long stage of the day Al had increased the lead by a further 20 seconds.

1, Belgrave 3:55:21; 2, Tipton 3:55:56; 3, Birchfield 3:57:25.

Fastest: A.Stewart (Belgrave) 27:11; N.Stirk (Tipton) 27:31; C.Cariss (Bingley) 27:33.

Stage 12

The margin was 35 seconds. Tipton’s Danny Gibbons was thought to be about on a par with our own Lee Hurst. For the first time, after almost four hours of racing, we felt fully confident that the race was ours. Photographer Mark Shearman said that he would be wanting to get the team together for a photograph and would our man be kind enough to celebrate as he went across the line. Our supporters began to come in from the course to witness the first ever Belgrave victory at Sutton Park. There was a little flutter when the announcer relayed the news that Gibbons had pulled back 5 seconds; but of course he had – he had nothing to lose – he had to go all out. Lee would be fine. What we didn’t know was that Lee’s heart had already been pumping in overdrive before he set out. It had been a long day of incredible tension.

Bud Baldaro’s voice sounded alarm bells. “They are at Keeper’s Pool and the Tipton man is just three seconds behind.” Tipton supporters still dotted around the course had been screaming themselves hoarse and their man was flying. The Belgrave team sprinted off towards the finishing straight to give their support. Approaching the final turn Gibbons took the lead. As they turned into the straight Hurst went ahead again. Now the headlight of the lead bike could be seen by those at the finish – and the runner immediately behind was – Tipton. Gibbons’ arm went up in a victory salute. He was 5th fastest of the day. They’d got it.

We can’t do better than return to the words of Will Cockerell (12th man at Milton Keynes) who knows what a last leg run is like.

“We all know, Lee could go back to Sutton Park tomorrow and run 15 to 20 seconds faster than he did today without breaking a sweat. But the pressure he was under – well, only he could know. I would have said it was four or five times the pressure that I had at Milton Keynes the other day. Half a mile into my stage that day, my legs had turned to jelly and that horrid feeling of nausea was overwhelming as I said to myself: “If the Bedford man catches me, I’ll have to let him go – I have no fight left.” I shared these sentiments with Lee after his run today and he said he had experienced every emotion that I was speaking of; and then some. He was running with the proverbial fridge on his back.”

"Southern" 12-Stage Road Relay

The tradition grows stronger

8 April 2001, SEAA 12-Stage Road Relay, Milton Keynes.

There’s a different atmosphere about the team these days. Not only do our runners have to fight to get into the team, they know that having got into the “twelve”, there will be medals at stake and the chance to make a name for themselves prior to the National team being selected; no-one wants to pull out in those circumstances. From the time that the team was picked the previous weekend right up until Will Cockerell carried our colours across the line in 3rd place not one man dropped out of the squad. We can never remember that happening before.

Belgrave last won the event in 1990 when the race was still being held in our own back yard at Wimbledon. The period following this, with the race moving to Thurrock in 1994-1998, proved to be a miserable time for the Bels. as we never got near the front of the field; but the move to Buckinghamshire coincided with an upswing in our fortunes and in the three years that the Open University and Milton Keynes AC have hosted the event we have not been out of the awards. The only trouble is – the gold gongs are still missing from our collection.

The entity formed from the amalgamation of Windsor, Slough & Eton AC and Borough of Hounslow AC did their best to wind us up with a derogatory statement on their t-shirts but our teams were far too intent on enjoying the race and the day to worry about them. Kids!

A pleasant surprise for the Men's Team Manager Alan Mead came at the end of the afternoon. The lads had wanted to show their appreciation of his efforts throughout the last few seasons and a collection resulted in the purchase of matching FILA hat and gloves, some programable postage scales to help him get his letters delivered on time and some wonderful IAAF statistical volumes to keep him occupied through the summer months. There were flowers for Patricia the "Cakes and Tea" lady, wine for Don "Wheels" Anderson and more for Bob Bridges who assisted with the driving to Durham for the National. Many thanks Team - you're a grand bunch - and a delight to work for.

Women's 6 Stage Race

It was great that we had a team in action in the SEAA Women’s 6-Stage event. Team Manager Catherine Eastham had managed to twist a few arms and although the Belles finished pretty well down the field – you’ve got to start somewhere. There must be a very good chance of picking up the most improved team award next year. Juliette Clarke, hitting great form with the London Marathon just two weeks away, ran a speedy 19:56 which was third fastest on her stage and 14th fastest overall.

An exceptional team effort in “National” – Hurst takes “Parker Bowl” again

24 February 2001, National Cross Country Champs., Durham

With the going good and conditions surprisingly bright when snow and rain had been threatened, an exceptional team effort gave the Bels. the top ten men’s team place they were looking for in the 2001 English National Cross Country Championships. Missing the services of those selected for World Cross Country Championship duties and with Charles Herrington back on the sidelines again with a confirmed stress fracture, hopes for a successful foray to Durham took another dive when Lloyd Catley went down with flu and Joachim Wolf was involved in a car crash on his way to the race. But our ten men lined up amongst the 1300 strong field hadn’t travelled 300 miles north to give a low-key performance.

As is often the case it was Paul Freary’s figure that was first spotted by the Belgrave supporters. Lying somewhere around 40th after the charge, he was closely followed by Lee Hurst – out to hold on to the Parker Bowl which is awarded to the first Belgrave man home. Al Stewart normally starts steadily and comes through the field with even-paced running but he too was well forward – around 70th at a rough count – with the rest of the Belgrave gang packing well in the mid hundreds. Already the team title looked like a three horse race between Tipton, Bingley and Morpeth.

It was a marvellous course for spectators who were able to dash from one zig-zag section to another to monitor Belgrave progress. On the second circuit Rob McHarg got away from Roger Alsop who had Will Cockerell close up behind him and Najibe Hliouat and non-scoring Malachi Byansi not far away. Nearer the front Lee Hurst had gone ahead of Paul but the revelation was Alaster Stewart, swiftly gaining on both of them. He was now in the early sixties and as Paul Freary sagged a little in mid race, Al came past and going out again for the final lap had his sights on Lee, now just a dozen places and perhaps eight seconds ahead.

At the front a leading bunch of ten or more had come down by now to just two men who tackled the final 3 kilometres almost side by side. Birchfield’s Mike Openshaw was perhaps the favourite to win but 21 year-old Sam Haughian of Hounslow seemed to be the man pushing on with most determination. The finish neared: Haughian continued to press hard but Openshaw was almost alongside him and in a most thrilling climax they entered the funnel side by side – until the Birchfield man switched gear to sprint away in the last 30 metres.

For Belgrave, Lee’s Hurst’s strength told in the end. He maintained his advantage on Al who nevertheless was delighted with his effort and could not resist raising an arm to signal his pleasure as he crossed the line in 56th. Paul had recovered from his mid-race bad patch and if anything was coming back at Al at the finish. Every one of the rest of the team ran well. Veteran Phil Carstairs was not pleased with his race after recently having the beating of a less than fit Roger Alsop but he was only 20 places off his position of the previous year. Meanwhile, Will and Roger had knocked spots off their previous best National runs, both of them improving with every running of the race.

A strong Shaftesbury Barnet team comfortably took the Finch-Wayte trophy for top Southern club away from us but our 8th team place was a terrific performance. If we can continue to place in the top ten on a regular basis then there are certainly going to be times ahead when we can raid the awards table.

At nine to score good old Don Anderson stepped into the breach. Don has run more Nationals than anyone else in the club with around a dozen to his name in claret and gold and good few more in his Surrey AC vest. The official results showed that we were also placed 8th at nine to score but the judges must have misread the number of someone from another club and instead of taking Don’s position, gave us a ninth man home some 250 places earlier. We should really have been 9th team.

Tania Sturton ran a good race to put herself up in the first third of the Senior Women’s field but it was a shame that she had no-one else to back her up. Debbie Hearn was also a lone Belgrave runner in the Under 20 Women’s event. Wouldn’t it be great to go to a “National” one day and see full Belgrave teams in all age groups – male and female.

"Sweatshop" Surrey League title returns to Thames H&H

23 scorers throughout the winter – but it’s 3rd place overall

3 February 2001, Surrey Cross Country League Division One, Race Four, Farthing Downs, Coulsdon.

We won’t bore you with too many details of illness and injury but suffice it to say that the fourth and last race in the Surrey League series for 2000-2001 gave a few more runners the chance to get into the scoring ten and the final tally showed that no fewer than twenty-three athletes had been on the score sheet throughout the winter. And we've had another twenty-three in Surrey League action who didn’t get into scoring positions this time round. With a broad base like this, regular success has just got to come along.

Thames Hare & Hounds consolidated their position at the top of the league with a third win while the Bels. could only make fourth on the day. Both South London and Herne Hill Harriers closed right up and the final result showed that while Thames were clear winners, a mere 20 points covered the next three clubs after all four matches and 20 miles of racing. Third place overall was our lot. Just 7 points fewer (we could have found them in two-dozen different ways) and we would have held on to second place.

Vice-Captain Alaster Stewart arrived at Heathrow on a jet from Hong Kong at 5am on the morning of the race to lead the Belgrave contingent home. He got the better of Cap’n Roger on the second circuit and both of them were keen to keep ahead of Phil Carstairs, celebrating his recently acquired veteran status with some terrific form. It was great to see Steve Clarke back in the team again after four or five months of problems; likewise “Gerry” Adams, away from the action for a similar period. They don’t come any grittier than Charlie Dickinson who, at nigh on 53 years of age, scored in his third out of three league runs this winter.

Down in the basement, West 4 Harriers were delighted to remain in the premier division after promotion from division two last season, while Croydon Harriers face relegation and Borough of Hounslow AC are expected to leave the League altogether to tackle the Chiltern League in forthcoming years as a combined Windsor, Slough, Eton & Hounslow outfit.

South of England Championships

27 January 2001, SEAA Cross Country Champs., Parliament Hill

So much for targets. For our men’s team this event was to have been the first of four events that we were to concentrate on. Our league campaign and winning streak in the South of Thames were forfeited for – a team position three places lower than last year.

Paul Freary, who lives 10 minutes from where the Northern Championships were being held, drove 200 miles each way to hit the Hill hard to go over the top in second place. He’d not been going as well as he’d have liked in training recently but after struggling on the first lap, after that powerful start, fought his way back and was satisfied with a place in the top 20.

It was another great run from Jason Lobo, who lives even closer to the Northern venue than Paul but travelled south to put himself to the test over that famous Parliament Hill mud. It was a morass, so thick in places that runners could hardly pull their feet out of it and yet here we had a 1:45 800m man coming home in 19th spot and ribbing Paul that he might have had a go at him if he’d not thought that it might upset him to see a half-miler come sailing past after 15 kilometres. Every one of the rest of the guys ran well, particularly Phil Carstairs who placed a best ever 62nd and would have been higher still but for a fall.

Teamwise, it was a chance missed. Thames Hare & Hounds were awesome with 6 in 44 – and they won the South of Thames the previous week and will almost certainly take the league as well.

Erica Fogg backed up her Surrey County run with another fine effort and with Tania Sturton and Syreeta Stracey in action we weren’t so far away from a full team. Fabien Bernard-Gaudin had to pull out of the Junior Men’s race; he broke a toe before Christmas and his recovery was not as complete as he had thought.

South of Thames win streak comes to an end

20 January 2001, South of Thames C.C. Championship, Roehampton.

After three consecutive team wins in this championship, and in spite of the fact that the race was held on (almost) home turf, the magnificent Dewar Shield found new keepers for the next twelve months.

It was a difficult situation. It would have been great to have extended our winning streak, and we certainly had enough men left who had not been barred from the event, but in the middle of a five week run of races something had to go - and this was it.

Steve Zealy was our only legitimate runner, in 62nd spot, but right up the front second-claimer Richard Ashe carried our colours to an outstanding win - although as a guest his name did not feature on the SoT result sheet. Fabien Bernard-Gaudin, still awaiting clearance to score for us, suffered a similar fate.

Top of page

Sparse turnout for Women's League

13 January 2001, Women’s Surrey C.C. League Race Three, Lightwater Park.

It was back to Lightwater for match three in the series. The race was scheduled to have been held in Richmond Park but the authorities deemed that with so much wet weather recently, the Park was likely to be damaged by the feet of so many harriers.

It was a very sparse turnout from our seniors who placed last on the day and now seem destined for division two again. After three matches the Belles lie in 9th place, although a good turn-out for the final race could save the day.

Things looked brighter in the younger age-groups, however, and both the under 13 and under 15 teams finished up in second place with Jessie Massey and Lizzie Hodges filling the two runners up slots in the younger race.

Top of page

Hammered at home !

13 January 2001, Surrey CC League Race 3, Wimbledon Common

With a huge absentee list we were always going to be up against the task of keeping close to, or even stealing a few more points away from, Thames Hare & Hounds, in our quest to retain the Surrey League title. Four top Belgrave runners were taking the chance of overseas or international standard competition, work commitments pulled away another four, injury accounted for two and communication breakdown took out a couple more. Still we lined up twenty-three men; and didn’t they battle magnificently to get us into 2nd place on the day. Frankly though, Thames were in great form and took full advantage of our weakened state.

Our second year of running on the new course revealed a few delights that we hadn’t expected: drifts of dried leaves in the woods hid a black porridge of the most glutinous variety. Even the team manager got a taste of this as, at the end of the day, he found himself the guardian of a pair of the most horrendously slimed Reeboks left behind by a Belgrave runner who couldn’t bear to put them in his kitbag.

Jason Lobo led the team home with Rob McHarg continuing his patch of good form (3rd in the Berkshire Champs. the previous week). Twenty-one year-old Richard Hayman made another advance up the order to place 16th and a betting man might well be advised to have a few bob on Rick’s chances of spending next winter’s series in the top ten. The middle order troops did us proud, running way above expectations, and especially welcome were new men Lloyd Catley and Guy Lavender – first Surrey League runs from them and both in the “ten”. As “Our Will” was heard to say whilst savouring his curry, “We might not have won and the league may be slipping away but it was one of the best ever efforts from a Belgrave team.”

So, is it out of sight? We’d have to say that chances of lifting the title for 2000-2001 look very slim!

Very many thanks to all those who marshalled, marked the course, judged, timed and helped with results. Particularly well done to Don Anderson: having laid out the trail he then had to remark it after someone attempted to sabotage the event by neatly removing every flag and trace of tape over a whole section of the route. Thank goodness for mobile ‘phones enabling the sending of a warning to hold back the senior race while the track was remarked.

Top of page

Low key at Lloyd Park

6 January 2001, Surrey Cross Country Championships, Lloyd Park.

Again we were unable to produce a strong presence for the County Championships. Hopes were high for a good placing in the youngest girls’ age group with Louise Collier having been in fine form in recent league races. On this occasion she was not at her best and when shaken by a severe slip, came out of the race altogether.

There were high hopes that Richard Ward would be able to duplicate his win of last year in the junior men’s race but the redoubtable talent of Reigate’s Ed Prickett prevailed. Richard is likely now to be switching his attentions to indoor track races before returning for the road relays. Running in the combined junior and under 17 women’s race Debbie Hearn placed 16th overall but only just missed the medals, being fourth junior to the line.

Our women’s team picked up bronze medals last year but from that squad only Tania Sturton was back on the course this time and filled exactly the same place – 25th. Up ahead new member Erica Fogg, yet another Dave Lucas trained athlete, showed that she is going to be a great asset to the team – when it gets together again – by running home in 10th place.

Shortly before the senior men’s race it had looked as if Belgrave were not going to be able to start a team with only four runners and spectating Don Anderson on the course with 10 minutes left before the pistol was due to be fired. Then Lloyd Catley arrived for his first ever run in Belgrave colours and Don was coerced into his kit to complete the six. Just as the runners were lining up Malachi Byansi arrived and with no warm up at all, joined the field to give us seven on the start line.

Herne Hill’s Dave Taylor continues to dominate cross country events in Surrey but in this Championship he did not have it totally his own way. In muddy conditions Taylor, Belgrave’s Kevin Nash and South London’s Stuart Major broke away early with Staines of South London not far behind. Kevin was totally focused on the race and for a while, as Major dropped back, it was the Belgrave Harrier who tended to be showing ahead as mud and water flew up from the leading pair’s flying feet.

Unfortunately a slight niggle in Kevin’s lower back, which had already caused him to cut short a training session during the week, flared up again and on the second of the three circuits Taylor prised open a gap which grew to about 20 seconds. Both runners were still going away from the rest of the field where all sorts of drama was taking place. Major fell; Staines and Herne Hill’s second scorer Boyle came through; Staines then had a stomach problem and dropped back alarmingly before finally making sure of a bronze medal at the very end of the race.

Our own Roger Alsop, short of training as a result of various injuries in recent months, started steadily and progressed through the field for a satisfactory 21st at the end. Malachi and Lloyd were within a few places of each other for most of the race. Both are gradually gaining fitness but in the end it was Mal who proved the strongest with Lloyd drifting back until he found himself under attack from Erwann Lemenager who was having a great run. It was good to see Steve Zealy back in action for the Bels. again – the 13 years since he formed part of our National team seem to have flown!

item.title: Women's Southern League 2001: Match 1, Battersea Park
item.dc:creator: belgravearchive
item.content:encoded:
Teams: 1 Belgrave 225.5; 2 Aldershot F&D 168; 3 South London H 136; 4 Croydon H 132; 5 St. Albans 108.5.

For the first time in a long time the Belles topped the league having amassed their highest points total ever (so far!) in a league match.

In terms of performance of the day, it’s difficult to decide where to begin. Shelley Drew’s new club record of 54.70 in the discus also happened to be a new stadium record (beating Judy Oakes’ 49.92). In addition, 5 more club records were broken on the day.

Michelle Nestor, showing even more promise this season, broke her own U17 triple jump record with 10.66 (an improvement of 22cms).

The seniors too had a good day, with Esther Erharuyi setting a new club best of 60.6 in the 400m hurdles, beating the 1990 previous of 65.7. Jennifer Culley equalled her own 400m club record of 55.2 and Sylvia Cruz added 4m to the Javelin club record with a throw of 47.16. Attempts at a new Portuguese record though were not met.

Club records aside there were many other outstanding performances from juniors and seniors and newcomers and ‘old-timers’. There were a total of 26 first places, 17 seconds, 6 thirds, 5 fourths and no lasts! Sadly though, such a wealth of talent means that there’s not enough room to comment on all of the fabulous results individually.

With such an excellent start, a great deal more promised, and the continuing great atmosphere and team spirit of the Belles, this season is looking exceedingly promising. Sir Eddie was entranced enough, despite the appalling weather, to stay and support the team for the whole day.

At Hayes stadium, Belgrave's junior men, winners of the National Junior League title last season, had a tough time, finishing third to Enfield & Haringey and Shaftesbury Barnet. Lawrence Oboh completed an impressive 100m/200m double in 10.8/21.7 seconds and outstanding 15 year-old Gary Wilson long-jumped 6.24 metres to win the B event. Prolific racer Richard Ward won the 800 metres in 1:54 but his hard weekend (he had run at Birmingham in the AAA 12-Stage Road Relay the dat before) caught up with him in the 1500m where he had to settle for second in 4:05. 'The Simpsons' had the measure of the 400m by winning both A and B races in 48.9 seconds and 53.0 seconds respectively.

item.title: Men's British Athletics League Division One - 2002: Match 1, Copthall Stadium
item.dc:creator: belgravearchive
item.content:encoded:
Anguish for the Team Managers - but Bels. win opening match

Every year we await the return of many of our team from various warm weather training camps with some trepidation. On average about 30% return injured. This year it seemed more like 80% as inquiry after inquiry brought forward another tale of woe.

Add to this the fact that the British Universities T&F Championships had been scheduled for the same weekend and the anguish of the Team Managers was pitiful to behold! In many events we were destined to run our 5th or 6th strings and fortunately for the team they all performed above expectations.

A measure of the problems was evident in the short sprints where long jumper Darren Thompson ran a creditable 10.93 but only to finish last in the A event while triple jumper Phillips Idowu bettered this with a 10.81 to finish a higher than expected second in the B 100m.

Sean Baldock moved down to the B 200m to win with a windy 21.43 sec and confirm to coach Mark Gregory that all was on target for a fast 400m. But the one lap event was suffering from a shortage of our more experienced members who were otherwise engaged at the BU Champs in Glasgow. So we blooded 18 year old Jon Simpson and 20 year old find Tim Bayley and to everyone's surprise they came up with the goods with two fine second places.

The damage limitation exercise was going well as we moved to the longer distance track events. Whereas in past years our middle distance squad had little depth we now have a fine collection of athletes two of whom made impressive debuts in the 800m. Both Neil Speaight in the A and Adam Zawadsky in the B got boxed and left themselves too much to do to catch winning Woodford Green men - Matt Shone and Andy Brown, both of whom kicked well at the right time. Impressively Shone doubled up in the 1500 and managed to outsprint Mark Miles. But another second spot was acceptable as we were beginning to realise that Woodford Green, who traditionally see-saw between Div. 1 and Div. 2 had been recruiting strongly in the winter. Strangely, Woodford were weak in the 5000m and Paul Freary's usual 4th spot in the A and Ric Hayman's 3rd place in the B moved us slightly ahead in the match score. A lead that was to be further extended as Kevin Nash pipped Lee Hurst in the steeplechase with Kevin third in the A and Lee first in the B.

Again, every year we believe Ian Wells won't make our premier team and each year he proves us wrong. No change in 2001 as our 39 year old gained 3 valuable points in the B high hurdles. In the A race, Erese of Woodford ran an impressive 13.84 with Neil Owen third in a windy 14.12 secs. Fortunately, Ian was not required to run the 400H where Jon Squirrel and 17 year old newcomer Andrew Bennett (2nd) acquitted themselves well. But Ian was press ganged into the long relay and seemed pleased with surviving a sub 55 sec effort.

Meanwhile, the field events, running in parallel with the track displayed a similar mix of fortunes. Mick Jones and Dave Smith - the two finest hammer throwers in the country - swept aside the opposition to get proceedings off to a fine start. Then two wins in the long jump with Darren Thompson hitting a legal 7.48m on his first attempt prior to nipping off to the 100m. Julian Flynn added good triple jump B points to his B long jump win with Phillips Idowu easily winning the A triple jump off a short run up.

The pole vault was an unmitigated disaster. Newham men won the A with only 4.70m and the B with just 4.60m. Meanwhile, in this exalted company we achieved precisely "nil point". Mile Edwards who had flown in from Texas for this one event was inconsolable. By now, Newham were making an impressive points surge. The javelin result took them ahead of Woodford Green but their inroads into our lead faltered as Kevin Brown and Lee Newman together collected 50 points from the shot and discus. Kevin, who had been dragged out of retirement for this match, declared himself highly delighted with his efforts, as too were the team managers.

It remained for us to get the baton round in both relays and victory seemed assured. Mind you the sprint relay team did not contain a single sprinter so there was just a little pre-race tension around as the techniques of baton changing were debated. Add to this the last minute replacement of Nick Dawson with Jon Simpson who was warming up for the long relay and you get the picture. And they finished 6th with a creditable 44.15sec time considering the poor changeovers.

So a fine win and excellent start to our 2001 campaign. But had we learnt enough for the team selection for the European Champion Clubs Cup in Madrid? We think not.

With only five Belgravians in action on the track it was left to the jumpers and throwers to keep the team afloat. Clifton Green, grandson of the late “Jimmy” Green, founder of Athletics Weekly and a former member of Belgrave, boosted the throws with a fine 61.62 javelin throw whilst James Hilston – no training but a winter of rugby playing behind him – took the high jump with 1.95. Outstanding in the middle-distance running events was Al Stewart whose first 5000m of the season gave him a chance to lap the entire field to win in a personal record; he followed up with a another maximum score in the 1500m where a late burst into the finishing straight took him from 4th to 1st.

item.content:encoded:

item.title: Women's Southern League 2001: Match 2, Handy Cross, Wycombe
item.dc:creator: belgravearchive
item.content:encoded:
Teams: 1 Belgrave 224; 2 Radley 173; 3 Salisbury 166; 4 Wycombe 143; 5 Medway 90.

There was plenty to catch the eye in match 2 where the Belles continued their quest for competition at a higher level. Two enormous senior club records set the tone but outstanding without setting a record was Captain Jennifer Culley, supposedly resting as much as possible for the following day’s Cup match but clocking up three wins (including her 55.0 effort in the long relay) against very strong opposition.

The records came from two debutantes. Diane Holden had the hammer judges covering a lot more ground than normal when she entered the circle to unleash throws in the 50 metre range. Her best of 53.98 added over 22 metres to our previous best. Meanwhile, on the track Kimberly Carson set the home stretch alight with a superb run in the sprint hurdles to remove eight whole tenths from a record that had stood for over twenty years. They both look like improving those marks in the near future.

Strong running came from Vicky Goodwin and Syreeta Stracey in the middle distance. Syreeta’s 400m and 1500m were both personal bests. Veteran Vilma Thompson and Vicki Hassell scored heavily in the throws while all-rounder Lisa Antill became another on our growing list of triple-jumpers; her 11.12 was an under 20 club record

Double wins came from under 15s Shereena McGregor and Louise Collier. In the 800m Louise took off like a gazelle and passed the bell in a startling 66 seconds by which time she was about 80m clear. A slightly slower first lap might have seen her get close to cracking 2:20. Hurdler Amy Forsyth was another to win by a mile and our under 17 300m hurdles best of 45.63 looks set for a revision before long.
